drills.title: vs Vijay-malu (823) — Three Knights Opening
drills.coachNote: White's whole point is Ne5-g6, forking your queen on e7 and rook on f8 in one move. By playing f6 you kicked the knight, but gave it that exact square — after Ng6 your queen scrambles to f7, then Nxf8 wins the rook outright, Rxf8 recapturing the knight but leaving you down the exchange, nearly four pawns swallowed. Rfe8 removes the fork first: with the rook off f8, g6 is just a retreat square, so the knight has nothing better than Nf3. Always check where an attacked piece can jump before you attack it.

drills.title: vs Vijay-malu (823) — Three Knights Opening
drills.coachNote: White's idea here isn't subtle — your knight on c6 has exactly one tempting central jump, and the f3-knight is sitting right on d4 waiting for it. When you played Nd4, Nxd4 exd4 opened the center, and suddenly White's queen swings over to g4, eyeing g7 and the king you haven't castled yet on e8 — you had to scramble with Qf6 just to cover things, costing most of your edge. Ne7 avoids all of it: it develops toward castling kingside without touching d4, and after c4 g6 Qb3 you're still comfortably equal. Before jumping a knight forward, check who already guards that square.

drills.title: vs belyjudegwapo (730) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's whole plan was d4, cracking open the center so the bishop on b2 finally gets to stare down that long diagonal at your king on g8, and the knight on f3 gets an outpost. Bd7 did nothing to stop that — after d4 exd4 Nxd4, White's knight lands right in the middle of the board and your position goes from crushing to merely okay, a swing of about three pawns. d5 was the move: grab the center yourself before White gets to. It even survives the scary-looking Bxh7+ Kxh7 Nxe5, because Bxe5 Bxe5 just trades pieces evenly and you're still completely winning. When you're up big, the center is still worth fighting for.

drills.title: vs belyjudegwapo (730) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's simplest hope here is just Rxa1 — your bishop sitting alone on a1 isn't defended by anything, and the rook on f1 can grab it the moment you give it a free move. That's exactly what Kxf8 did: by recapturing on f8 right away you left the bishop hanging for another turn, and Rxa1 picked it up for nothing, shrinking your huge +7 advantage by almost two pawns. Bd4+ solves it with a tempo — the bishop swings back onto the a1-g1 diagonal and checks the king, forcing Kh1, and only then do you play Kxf8 to recapture, bishop safely rerouted. Even in a crushing position, check for pieces you're about to abandon before making the 'obvious' recapture.
drills.threat: Your bishop on a1 is undefended — White's rook on f1 can just scoop it up for free.

drills.title: vs bbaldy87 (319) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Black's simple idea is Bxg5 — your bishop on g5 is hanging to the bishop on h6, and nothing of yours covers that square. Re1 develops a rook but ignores that, so after Bxg5 Nxg5 the trade itself is even, but the knight you recapture with lands right on the open g-file, where Rg8 pins it down, and you end up burning a tempo on f4 just to keep it alive — about a pawn and a half of your advantage gone to nothing. Bh4 sidesteps all of it: the bishop steps out of attack while staying active on the kingside, and you continue naturally with Nbd2 and Bg3 without ever handing Black that extra tempo. Before developing a new piece, check whether one you already have is under attack.
drills.threat: Your bishop on g5 is attacked by Black's bishop on h6, and nothing of yours currently guards that square.

drills.coachNote: White's pawn on e4 is one move from e5, and that push grabs a tempo on anything sitting on f6 — which is exactly where Qf3 is also pointed. Nf6 walks right into that: after e5 the knight's attacked, and if you're not careful about which piece needs to move, developing the other knight with Nc6 instead leaves the f6-knight hanging — exf6 just wins it outright, which is most of that 3.3 pawn swing. Nc6 on move two avoids the whole problem: it develops a piece e5 can't touch, and after Nh3 h6 c3 e5 Bc4 you're in a normal, playable position. When a pawn push is coming, don't put a piece on the square it attacks.

drills.coachNote: Here the real prize is White's king, stuck on e1 and unable to castle, and your bishop on f8 has a totally free diagonal down to b4 to check it right now. Qe5 centralizes the queen but gives White a spare tempo, and after a3 the Bb4+ idea just dies — axb4 would eat the bishop — so you let a chunk of your advantage slip away, about a pawn and a half. Bb4+ is what keeps the pressure on: it forces Nc3 to block, then Bxc3+ bxc3 Qxc3+ scoops up the c3 pawn with another check, dragging the king to f2 while you stay completely in control. When the enemy king hasn't castled, checks that stop it from tidying up are usually worth more than quiet centralizing moves.

drills.coachNote: Your rook on c1 shares the c-file with Black's king on b8 and queen on d7 — that's the real tension here. Qb3 looks natural, but it quietly abandons your queen's guard of the bishop on d3; Black takes it with Bxd3, and even though Nxa7+ Kxa7 Qxb4 wins back the knight, the position still swings hard against you. Rc7 is the shot that matters: sacrificing the rook drags the queen off d7, and after Qxc7 Nxc7 you've won the queen for a rook. Bxd3 Re1 Kxc7 follows, and you're still well ahead. Before moving a defender, always check what it's holding up.
